picked.t: 2 South Koreans jailed for beating compatriot restaurant owner to death in Ho Chi Minh City
picked.body: The Ho Chi Minh City People's Court on Sept. 4 sentenced Kim Jin, 31, to life in prison and Kang Yo Han, 30, to 20 years for murder. The victim, a South Korean restaurant owner, died after Kim struck him in the head with a metal canister containing nitrous oxide. A South Korean manager at the restaurant was also attacked and survived with injuries that resulted in an 87% disability, the court heard. The incident occurred early on Dec. 28, 2024, after Lee Chang Dae, a friend of Kim, and three other South Koreans went to the restaurant on Tran Hung Dao Street to drink and sing karaoke. At around 2:30 a.m., Lee damaged an LED screen in the karaoke room. A dispute broke out when an employee asked him to pay for the damage. The restaurant owner and manager went to the room to resolve the dispute, but a fight followed. The manager called police, while one of Lee's friends contacted Kim and told him the group "had gotten into trouble." Kim then asked Kang to accompany him to the restaurant. The two had been drinking at a nearby pub on Bui Vien Street. By the time they arrived, local police and security personnel were already at the restaurant. Kim allegedly grabbed a rubber baton from a patrol member before entering the room with Kang. The two then locked the door and attacked the owner and manager. Kim struck the owner in the head with the nitrous oxide canister, causing him to collapse. He had died by the time police broke into the room. At trial, Kim admitted attacking the victims but said he could not clearly remember what happened. He said he did not know why his friends were in trouble when he received the message. "I was not in a sober state at the time of the incident," he told the court. The jury board said the defendants had committed the crime in a violent manner and caused "particularly serious consequences." It also said they had attacked two people despite not knowing the reason for the original dispute. Kim received the heavier sentence because he was the one who asked Kang to go to the restaurant. The court also ordered the defendants to jointly pay more than VND5 billion (US$190,000) to the deceased's family and more than VND3 billion to the injured manager, after deducting more than VND1.3 billion already paid in compensation. Both men apologized to the victims and their families in their final statements.

picked.t: Vietnamese fruit gains stronger foothold in global markets
picked.body: Held at AsiaWorld-Expo in Hong Kong on Sept. 2–4, the event features 730 exhibitors from 40 countries and territories. The Vietnamese delegation, organized by the Vietnam Fruit and Vegetable Association, comprises 24 booths representing 22 businesses nationwide. The trade fair serves as a platform connecting businesses, distributors and consumers, with products and services spanning fruit, machinery, logistics, smart agricultural solutions and technologies. Dang Phuc Nguyen, the associationa's secretary general, said the Vietnamese delegation has expanded steadily over the years, from 10 businesses in 2017 to 22 this year. At Asia Fruit Logistica 2025, Vietnamese firms signed contracts worth about US$5 million directly with international partners. Revenue is expected to be higher this year, driven by key products such as durian, passion fruit and dragon fruit. He noted that the scale and export value of Vietnam's participation remain modest compared to the country's huge fruit and vegetable potential. The event brings broader benefits by helping Vietnamese businesses find partners, expand markets and promote the quality and reputation of the country's fruit industry. According to Nguyen, the fair also features technologies for harvesting, processing, preservation and transportation, particularly smart, organic and environmentally friendly farming solutions. Vietnamese businesses can explore these technologies for potential imports or technology transfers to improve the quality and value of agricultural products. Le Minh Tuan, director of Pulimex Import-Export, said his company is displaying Vietnamese specialties including dragon fruit, coconut, banana, longan, rambutan and mango, mainly to seek partners and expand export markets. After four consecutive participations, he said he considered the Hong Kong fair an important platform for Vietnamese fruit exporters to reach markets not only in Asia but also in the U.S., Europe, Australia, the Middle East and Africa. He also appreciated stronger support from Vietnamese authorities in addressing legal procedures and payment-related difficulties. Le Huu Dung, director of Vinafood International, which exports Vietnamese fruits to India and the Middle East, expressed hope that the event will help the company expand into other potential markets, backed by the diversity and growing reputation of Vietnamese fruit. Alessandro Cordano from Portugal said he was impressed by the variety of Vietnamese fruits , describing them as attractive in appearance, delicious, and beneficial to health. Vietnam's fruit and vegetable exports have grown strongly in recent years, rising from about $7 billion in 2024 to $8.6 billion in 2025 and expected to surpass $10 billion this year.

picked.t: Vietnam gains market share as China’s 3rd biggest vegetable, fruit supplier
picked.body: China spent approximately US$2.16 billion importing vegetables, flowers, roots, and fruits from Vietnam, up 19.3% from the same period in 2025, according to data from China Customs. Vietnam’s share rose from 13.8% of China’s imports in the first half of 2025 to almost 16% to rank behind Thailand (37%) and Chile (17%). Vietnam’s rise has been driven by both scale and changes in its product mix, with durian emerging as the biggest growth driver. This year, China has paid nearly $988 million for imports of fresh and frozen durian from Vietnam, up 43% from the same period a year earlier.thos Shipments of coconut also rose sharply but of mango, dragon fruit, and banana declined. Dang Phuc Nguyen, secretary-general of the Vietnam Fruit and Vegetable Association, said the proximity allows fresh products from Vietnam to reach China quickly, maintain better quality, and incur lower logistics costs than exports from Southeast Asia and South America. This advantage is particularly important for fresh fruits, which are highly dependent on transportation time. As demand for tropical fruits in China expands from major cities to second- and third-tier cities and provinces in the country’s northern and western regions, suppliers located closer to China have greater room for growth. China’s approval for a growing number of Vietnamese fruits has enabled businesses to expand their growing areas and output. But China is also imposing increasingly stringent requirements on imports. Nguyen said China is tightening oversight across areas ranging from business registration and growing-area codes to packing facilities. Origin fraud, the misuse of growing-area codes, and pest contamination can result in codes being temporarily suspended or revoked, directly affecting the exports of an entire growing region, he said.

picked.t: Why some Vietnamese workers are afraid to leave the office on time
picked.body: Official hours at Uyen’s private company in HCMC end at 5:30 p.m., but the 32-year-old marketing employee says she now routinely stays until after 7:30 p.m. or waits for her manager to leave first. She used to go home on time until a performance review two years ago, when she received an A- rating and a bonus US$192 lower than those of several colleagues. Her department head told her points had been deducted for her "work attitude" because she did not stay late like others and was therefore seen as less enthusiastic. "I don’t know when leaving work on time started being seen as a lack of dedication," Uyen says. Van Vy, 29, an IT employee in Hanoi, had a similar experience after failing to secure a salary increase in 2025. Although his job performance was good, his supervisor said he did not appear to be putting in enough effort because he "stood up to leave at 5:30 p.m. every single day." Vy has since adjusted his routine, spending more time over coffee in the morning and deliberately pushing work into the afternoon so he can remain at the office until around 7 p.m. The issue has become a frequent topic of debate on social media. One video discussing employees who leave as soon as working hours end drew 4.3 million views, while another debate over whether leaving on time reflects low emotional intelligence attracted nearly 270,000 viewers. Hundreds of posts have also appeared on Threads under the theme of being unable to leave work on time. Opinions are divided. Some argue that leaving on schedule after completing assigned tasks is professional, while others see an unwillingness to stay late as a sign of weak commitment. A VnExpress survey in August 2026 found that 13% of businesses assessed employees partly on the amount of time they spent in the office. Another poll of 2,000 readers found that 13% of workers finished their tasks on time but stayed behind because they feared being judged. This pressure to remain visible at work, even when productivity has dropped, is often described as presenteeism. A survey by U.K.-based health and wellbeing company Vitality found that presenteeism reduced productivity far more than absenteeism, costing an estimated 35 working days per employee each year. Still, some managers defend the practice. Thanh Toan, 45, director of an import-export company in Hai Phong, prefers employees to stay late because their physical presence can make coordination between departments easier and allow problems to be handled more quickly. He also believes voluntarily remaining after hours can signal responsibility, commitment and a willingness to put collective goals ahead of personal interests. Dr. Le Trung Hieu, deputy head of the human resource management department at the School of Business Administration, Vietnam National University, Hanoi, says Vietnam’s workplace culture has been shaped partly by its economic history and by increasing integration with East Asian business practices. "Foreign investment from East Asian countries have brought with it a work environment that emphasizes hierarchy, obedience to superiors, and consensus, along with fierce competitive pressure." Hieu adds that the reluctance to leave on time is also rooted in a widespread workplace assumption that longer hours reflect greater dedication. When companies lack clear performance indicators, managers may fall back on time spent at the office as a proxy for commitment, he says. From a psychological perspective, experts say some managers prefer to keep employees physically visible because it gives them a greater sense of control. Employees, meanwhile, may avoid leaving early because they fear conflict, being seen as less capable or losing promotion opportunities. Nguyen Thi Kieu Chinh, a financial adviser at FIDT Investment Consulting and Asset Management Joint Stock Company, says the phenomenon is particularly common in finance, technology and consulting in major cities, where daily output can be difficult to quantify. "Many people accept staying late because they fear appearing unmotivated or missing out on promotion opportunities," she says. But she warns that this kind of superficial display of commitment only offers short-term reassurance. Over time, it can erode motivation, increase staff turnover and drive away capable employees. It can also damage health and work-life balance. "A competitive economy is not built on the number of hours worked, but on the value generated during each hour," Chinh says. In Hanoi, sales manager Minh Phong, who oversees 20 employees, says he stopped judging staff by how late they stayed after realizing it did not improve performance. "I manage by deadlines for task completion, not by watching over adults like a preschool teacher," he says. Hieu recommends that businesses shift toward output-based management, establish transparent KPI systems and require employees to communicate progress clearly. picked.t: CEO of Vietnam International Financial Center in HCMC could get $32,000 monthly salary
picked.body: The proposal is included in a submission by the city People's Committee to the People's Council, the legislature, on salaries, benefits, and bonuses for personnel working in the management of the financial center (VIFC-HCMC). Other top executives and specialists and advisers could be paid salaries ranging from tens to hundreds of millions of dong a month. Salaries for other employees too could reach hundreds of millions of dong. The VIFC-HCMC was launched in February 2026 with the goal of developing a financial services ecosystem, attracting international capital and connecting Vietnam's financial market with global markets. A 2026 Vietnamese salary survey by Navigos Group found that CEOs and general directors of financial services, insurance, and securities companies earned VND184-419 million a month. At the VIFC-HCMC, the proposed VND100-180 million salary for the CEO is also higher than the VND86-141 million range for marketing and communications directors and department heads, the survey found. But the proposed VND30-60 million salary for specialists is broadly in line with the VND18-61 million range for experienced specialists in finance and accounting. The People's Committee said the market-based salary regime is intended to attract personnel with professional expertise, foreign language skills, international experience, and knowledge of international finance. The management agency is classified as a special administrative body responsible for directly running, licensing, and overseeing investment and financial business activities within the financial center while also carrying out new and complex functions in Vietnam. Its personnel are currently paid under the existing salary system, but the city government admitted that the highest salary of just VND11.6 million per month is not competitive enough to attract talent in international finance. The management agency has been using its regular operating budget to pay salaries since February 2026, but with the funding expected to last only another two months, the city government warned that without a special salary and remuneration mechanism being issued in time, 88% of employees face the risk of not being paid salaries, potentially causing resignations. For the chairperson and vice chairperson of the agency, who concurrently serve in other positions, the proposal is for an additional 50% on top of their salaries. Government workers deputed to work at the agency will also receive an additional allowance equivalent to 50% of their salary. The total annual cost of the proposed salaries, benefits, and bonuses is estimated at VND99.648 billion. It will initially be paid by the city, and once the financial center generates revenues, it will share the cost with the city.

picked.t: Holiday ‘bed rotting’ leaves young people more exhausted than refreshed
picked.body: Pham Ha, 25, an office worker in Hanoi’s Cau Giay area, barely left her home during the break. She stayed up scrolling through social media until 3 a.m., slept until 2 p.m., ate just one meal a day and then went back to bed. Before the holiday starting Aug. 29, she deleted her work messaging apps and silenced her phone. "Weeks of working late into the night to meet back-to-back deadlines had worn me out. Once the holidays came, all I wanted was to lie still, see no one and think about nothing," she says. By the final day, however, she was aching all over and suffering from headaches and dizziness, and, instead of feeling refreshed for the week ahead, she felt worse. Minh Thu, 27, a communications worker in Hanoi, also spent most of the holidays in bed at her parents’ house in central Nghe An Province. Just fighting the crowds for a ticket and traveling more than 300 kilometers home had exhausted her. So she canceled plans for outings with friends and family, confined herself to her room where she ate in bed, watched movies, listened to music, and slept. "By the time I returned to the city for work, my mind was blank. I felt more sluggish and tired than before," she says, Ha and Thu are among a growing number of young people embracing "bed rotting," a term that originated on TikTok for spending days on end in bed to escape work pressures and social interactions. In a VnExpress survey of nearly 1,000 readers, 34% said they regularly engaged in bed rotting on days off. U.S. research firm Morning Consult found that 49% of Gen Z did so regularly or occasionally, compared with 41% of millennials. Among Gen Z, 62% had canceled social plans just to stay in bed, with 53% saying they felt guilty or empty afterward. Dr. Nguyen Viet Chung, head of the mental health department at Hanoi’s E Hospital, says the behavior has clear psychological roots in pressure to perform, hit KPIs, and meet social expectations, which could keep young people in a constant state of stress. A 2023 UNICEF report said that 20% of adolescents in Vietnam faced mental health issues, while a NielsenIQ survey found that 65% of young people felt pressured to outperform their peers. Against this backdrop, Chung says sleeping in, reading, and unplugging from work for a single weekend day could help the body recover, but when the inactivity stretches into a third or fourth day, the line between recharging and avoiding reality begins to disappear. "At a certain point, staying in bed is no longer rest. When people begin to lose motivation and feel guilty but still cannot get themselves off the mattress, the behavior has become an unhealthy coping mechanism. It may even be an early sign of anxiety or depression." He lists three physical effects of staying in bed for prolonged periods: Disrupted sleep-wake cycle: Sleeping out of sync with the body's natural day-night rhythm disrupts hormone release, leaving people drowsy by day and unable to sleep at night. Poorer circulation: Inactivity slows metabolism. After several days, muscles and joints stiffen, leaving people feeling even more fatigued. Constant stimulation of the cerebral cortex: Using a phone in bed prevents the brain from fully resting and erodes the association between bed and sleep, potentially leading to sleep disorders. "People need to know the difference between allowing themselves to rest and no longer having enough energy to function. The two may look similar, but they are fundamentally different." To make time off truly restorative, he recommends keeping a consistent wake time, sleeping seven to eight hours a night, and avoiding long daytime naps to catch up on lost sleep. He also advises reserving the bed for sleep and taking activities such as reading and phone scrolling elsewhere. Rather than stay glued to a screen, young people should interrupt their scrolling with a short activity every two hours, spend 15-30 minutes in sunlight each day, and do some light exercise, he says. After once finding that oversleeping left him exhausted, Tuan Minh, 24, of HCMC, decided to structure his days off differently this year. He woke at 7 a.m., ran for 30 minutes, cooked three meals a day and spent time reading. "Work keeps me busy and makes me eat at irregular hours. I used the holiday to get back to a healthier routine," he says.

picked.t: 4 doctor passengers, nurse deliver premature baby on Vietnam flight from Denmark
picked.body: None of them was an obstetrician. But as Dr. Ho Khanh Thanh of the general planning department at Cho Ray Hospital, one of the five who helped deliver the baby, put it: "There was little time to worry in an emergency. I focused only on helping the mother deliver safely and preparing for possible complications." Speaking to VnExpress on the afternoon of Sept. 6, Thanh said the unexpected situation occurred at around 1 a.m. that day on Vietnam Airlines flight VN38 from Copenhagen, Denmark, to HCMC. The plane had been in the air for about 10 hours, with around two hours remaining before it was due to touch down, when a Vietnamese passenger who was 30 weeks pregnant suddenly showed signs of labor. Chief flight attendant Vu Hai Anh made an announcement asking for someone with medical expertise to provide assistance. Besides Thanh, there was a Vietnamese cardiologist and pediatrician each and the foreign doctor and nurse, all of whom immediately came to the passenger's aid. The five quickly assigned tasks among themselves. Medical gloves, disinfectants and other medical supplies are available on all aircraft. At first, Thanh thought the passenger might simply be extremely anxious. However, her abdomen was contracting strongly, her water had broken and he could feel the baby's head. The group determined that she was genuinely in labor and needed immediate attention. Delaying the delivery could have increased the risk of respiratory problems for the baby. The flight crew moved the passenger to the business-class cabin, where there was more space. The passenger spoke several languages and remained calm, communicating and cooperating with the doctors. For Thanh, this was a premature delivery under conditions completely different from those in a hospital, with no delivery room, resuscitation equipment or obstetric team available. The last time he had personally assisted with a delivery in the emergency department at Cho Ray Hospital was some 12 years ago. The woman was instructed to hold her breath, push with the contractions and cooperate with the doctors. Within six or seven minutes, the baby was born. The medical team immediately kept the baby warm and monitored its breathing. Without the equipment available in a hospital, they made use of items on the aircraft. They placed the baby skin-to-skin on the mother’s chest and cut the mother’s shirt to position the baby against her chest, both to promote contact with the mother and help keep the newborn warm. Without a specialized cord tie, the doctors used a mask strap from a sterile package to tie the umbilical cord before cutting it. The nurse established an intravenous line and administered fluids to the mother. Her blood pressure was around 110/70 mmHg. The baby was crying and breathing well. Mother and baby were temporarily stable, but the doctors had to determine nevertheless what to do next. The aircraft was more than two hours from Vietnam, while the 1.3-kilogram newborn needed immediate neonatal care. Emergency landing in Myanmar Thanh said he told the medical team and flight crew that if they continued to Vietnam, Cho Ray Hospital's emergency team could be ready to assist when the aircraft landed, but being in the air for more than two more hours posed a risk to the premature baby. The medics considered two options for a quick landing: Bangkok in Thailand and Yangon in Myanmar. Bangkok was about one hour and 20 minutes away but the airport had already granted permission for the plane to land. Yangon was 20 minutes away, but discussions took longer before Myanmarese authorities agreed to allow the aircraft to make an emergency landing. The aircraft landed in Yangon, where the mother and baby were taken to a hospital. After refueling, the plane continued its journey to HCMC, landing at 6:05 a.m. Speaking to VnExpress , chief flight attendant Hai Anh said the airline's representative in Myanmar had informed them that "the mother and baby are safe and healthy." "This was the first time in my nearly 30 years in the profession that I had witnessed a passenger give birth on a flight. The delivery happened very quickly. I only felt reassured when I heard the baby cry," she said, adding that she was impressed by the mother's composure and courage. "Although she was somewhat worried, she remained very calm and followed the doctors' instructions." According to a Vietnam Airlines spokesperson, the emergency landing was a timely and necessary decision given the exceptional circumstances, and it was one of several cases in which the airline had made emergency landings this year to assist passengers requiring medical attention. On June 24, a flight from Ho Chi Minh City to Shanghai made an emergency landing in Hong Kong. On Jan. 7, a flight from Frankfurt to Hanoi also made an emergency landing in Kolkata in India. picked.t: Durian exports expected to hit $4B this year
picked.body: Dang Ngoc Diep, deputy minister of Agriculture and Environment, said at the government's regular press conference on Thursday that durian is one of the agricultural products with relatively high value, a cultivation area of about 200,000 hectares and an output of approximately 2.08 million tonnes. It is a key crop of the agriculture sector, accounting for about 40% of its total export turnover. In the first eight months, durian exports were estimated at $1.95 billion, of which exports to China alone accounted for $1.85 billion or 95%. In response to difficulties facing the fruit’s exports, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment has sent working delegations led by deputy ministers to work directly with localities, particularly high-output growing areas in the Central Highlands, the southeastern and southwestern regions, and Dong Nai province, to remove bottlenecks, Diep said. On July 1, the ministry launched origin tracing through its electronic system. "We met with the trade counsellors of the US and China. They highly appreciated the ministry's implementation of origin tracing for the first time and its efforts to promote Vietnamese agricultural products as reputable brands domestically and internationally," Diep said, noting that this is one of the solutions to boost exports and increase the value of durian. The ministry has also worked to address difficulties and obstacles related to the issuance of growing-area codes. "All durian growing areas are now decentralised, allowing ward- and commune-level authorities to issue growing-area and packing-facility codes, making the process more convenient," he said. Following a meeting between ministry leaders and the Chinese side on Aug. 14, the General Administration of Customs of China granted 567 growing-area codes for Vietnamese durian, bringing the total number to more than 1,800. The deputy minister also pointed out several limitations in the durian sector, including rapid growth that has not yet been matched by the organization of value chains. In addition, technical and market requirements are becoming increasingly stringent. He also highlighted challenges from international competition, noting that countries such as Malaysia and Thailand have introduced policies to promote durian exports to China . Regarding measures to be implemented, the ministry will step up trade promotion and diversify export markets, including continuing negotiations to expand access and increase share in promising markets such as India, Australia and New Zealand. In July, India agreed to allow Vietnam to export durian to its market. This is a market of more than one billion people with very strong demand in the coming period. Works are underway to expand export promotion activities in India, he said. The second measure is to reorganize production and develop sustainable raw-material areas, while reviewing production-area planning to ensure compatibility with land, water resources, climate and infrastructure conditions. The third is to standardize quality, food safety and origin tracing while improving research, application and transfer of science and technology, as well as digital transformation. The two other measures are developing storage, processing and logistics infrastructure; and expanding and strengthening the capacity of the laboratory system.

picked.t: Former Bamboo Airways chairman barred from leaving Vietnam over $1.7M tax debt
picked.body: The Gia Lai provincial tax authority said it sent a notice on Sept. 3 to the Immigration Department under the Ministry of Public Security requesting the temporary exit ban. Sam was identified as the beneficial owner of Bamboo Airways. As of Sept. 3, the airline owed more than VND44.06 billion in taxes to the provincial tax authority. Officials said the restriction could be lifted once Bamboo Airways settles the outstanding debt through the National Public Service Portal. Under Vietnamese regulations, a beneficial owner is an individual who ultimately owns or controls a company, including someone who directly or indirectly holds at least 25% of its charter capital or voting shares. Sam joined Bamboo Airways in 2022 and soon became its largest shareholder. He served as chairman from July 2023 to February 2024 before moving to the position of standing vice chairman. He returned as chairman in August 2025. About a month later, the investor group he represented transferred the airline back to property developer FLC Group, its former owner. At the time, Sam said the financial and managerial demands of continuing to own and operate Bamboo Airways had exceeded the investor group’s capabilities. He also pledged to take responsibility for the airline’s operating performance during its restructuring period. Sam stepped down as chairman in mid-November 2025 but remained a member of Bamboo Airways’ board of directors. He is also general director and legal representative of Viet Bamboo Airways Cargo JSC and several other companies linked to Bamboo Airways. Nearly a year after returning to FLC’s management, Bamboo Airways continues to face serious operational difficulties. The airline is currently operating just one aircraft and has suspended regular domestic services.
